newsitem.title: UK: Cargill tests soy in Britain after sabotage claim.
newsitem.headline: Cargill tests soy in Britain after sabotage claim.

text.p: U.S. grain giant Cargill was on Wednesday testing tanks of soybean oil at its plant near Liverpool, northwest England, after protesters against genetically modified crops claimed they had contaminated them.

The claims were made anonymously in letters sent to several British journalists on Tuesday. Paul Conway, vice president of Cargill's European oilseed processing division, said in a statement the company had not received any direct communication from the people claiming to have carried out the sabotage.
"But as food safety is involved, we are taking the claims seriously," he added.

All the vegetable oil storage tanks at the plant near Liverpool had been tested. "We are relieved that the initial testing shows no indication of contamination, but we will conduct more in-depth tests in the next few days," Conway said.
Cargill had alerted its customers to the claims and stopped shipments until all tests have been completed.
Conway said that the anonymous letter called on Cargill to stop importing from the United States soybeans that had been genetically modified to resist a herbicide used on crop fields.

Environmental activists in Britain were worried about the health implications of such a product and, at the very least, wanted supermarkets to label food that may contain genetically modified soya and corn.

US exporters do not separate modified and "natural" beans. "I would like to stress again that genetically modified soybeans have passed all safety approvals in the European Union as well as in Canada, Japan and the U.S.," Conway said.
"The UK authorities have approved both the soybeans and their products. We would not be handling these beans if they did not have full regulatory safety approvals," he added.
Environmental group Greenpeace has campaigned in both the U.S. and Britain against shipments of the modified soy, but British spokesman Adam Wolf said: "It wasn't us."
It was not part of Greenpeace's culture to act anonymously, he said.
Soy oil is used in a wide range of food products, including bread and margarine. Cargill, a privately-owned commodity trader, is one of the largest manufacturers in Britain.
